layer0_index.name: Section Two: The Intervening Years
layer0_index.description: Iron Arrow during the Great Depression and World War II.
subsections: World War II and an Iron Arrow Pow-Wow
layer0_index.one_sentence_summary: Section Two: The Intervening Years: Iron Arrow during the Great Depression and World War II. (2 subsections)

layer1_summary.paragraph: The years between Iron Arrow's founding and the post-war era tested the society's resilience against the backdrop of two of the twentieth century's most disruptive events, the Great Depression and World War II, while also preserving early traditions and memories that shaped the organization's identity. This section draws on firsthand accounts and historical records to illuminate how Iron Arrow survived periods of institutional strain and how its early customs — rooted in genuine respect for Native American culture — were sustained even as the university and the nation faced crisis. The narrative bridges the optimism of the founding era with the sobering realities that followed.
bullets: The early photographic record of Iron Arrow, including the masked founding members in the 1927 Ibis yearbook, reflects a sincere adherence to Native American spiritual beliefs about the camera capturing one's spirit, a custom continued for many years within the society.

Founding member Houghtaling provided crucial oral history explaining that the masks worn in tribal photographs were not meant to hide identities from fellow students but to honor the Indian belief that being photographed could harm one's spirit.

Member Larry Catha's 1925 account of traveling from Louisiana to Miami by truck captures the frontier character of early Florida and the pioneering spirit shared by the university community that gave birth to Iron Arrow.

The Great Depression placed significant financial and organizational pressure on the University of Miami and its student organizations, threatening the continuity of traditions that Iron Arrow had worked to establish in its first decade.

World War II further disrupted campus life and Iron Arrow's activities, as students and faculty were drawn into military service, making the society's survival and the preservation of its pow-wow traditions a meaningful act of institutional memory.

layer2_details.text:
THE GREAT DEPRESSION

- The University of Miami campus during the Depression era was known as "Cardboard College" — a facility that replaced the original grand, 
 plans for the University of Miami
- The original spectacular University plans collapsed along with the financial bust of the country, construction getting only as far as the skeleton of what is now the Merrick building
- One student account (unnamed narrator) describes entering "Cardboard College on September 24, 1934"
- Direct description of physical conditions: "The walls really were cardboard; the third floor really was unfinished; the outer walls really were a mess"
- Students physically participated in maintaining the building: "I really was one of those who got on a ladder and painted the building"
- The University's survival during this period is attributed to Dr. B. F. Ashe: "The existence of the University of Miami is due to Dr. Ashe's refusal to give up his dream, even using his own insurance money when in a bind"
- Women's dormitory at 624 Santander housed 34 women initially, growing to 64 by the time the narrator graduated
- Dorm operated under strict "in loco parentis" rules: sign in/sign out, grounding for being late, written permission required for overnight stays away
- House parents were identified as "Mom and Pop Koch"
- Student activities during this era included founding of Nu Kappa Tau (Women's honorary, later Mortar Board), founding of Theta Chi Omega Jewish sorority (sponsored by Alpha Epsilon Phi, became Alpha Eta chapter of AEPhi), writing for the Hurricane, editing the Ibis, and serving as president of Panhellenic
- Dr. Ashe asked the narrator (who graduated cum laude) to stay on as his executive secretary upon graduation

EARLY IRON ARROW HISTORY AND CONTEXT (BITS AND PIECES)

- First Iron Arrow photograph appears on page 190 of the 1927 Ibis
- Nine founding members wore specially made shirts and had already acquired a small tom-tom, which remained in use for at least the next 25 years
- The Iron Arrow arrow had not yet been returned from the foundry in downtown Miami where it was made at the time of the photograph; it was depicted in a black and white drawing made by Betty Weakley
- The drawing below the arrow profile depicted "a Seminole standing in his canoe, poling it into the distance over a bright horizon of water"
- Each of the founding nine wore a small, dark mask over his eyes in the photograph
- Masks were not worn to conceal identity from fellow students — each member's Iron Arrow membership was clearly listed beside his class photo elsewhere in the same yearbook
- Francis Houghtaling provided the explanation for the masks, stated as an afterthought: "One thing that they did not like was their pictures taken - hence our masks"
- The belief underlying the mask practice: "The belief was prevalent in Indian societies that part of the 'spirit' of the individual was captured forever by the film, to his detriment when body and spirit must part"
- Masks were worn "to conceal the identity of the wearer not from his fellow men, but from the camera"
- Iron Arrow member Larry Catha wrote his recollections in 1974; letter to Rhea Warren dated July 11, 1975
- Larry Catha was "the student who 'kicked off' the first football in the first football game the University ever played"
- Catha's journey to South Florida: departed Kentwood, Louisiana on December 27, 1925 at 3:30 a.m. Thursday in a new Ford truck
- Route traveled: Highway 90 / "old Spanish Trail"; crossed approximately 20 toll bridges; passed through Pensacola, Tallahassee, Madison, Lake City, Gainesville, Ocala, Orlando, Indian River City, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Dania, Hollywood, Lemon City, Buena Vista (now North Miami), Miami
- Suwanee River flood obstacle: arrived at flooded bridge 10:30 a.m., did not cross until 3:30 p.m. — "one driving, and one on each fender with a pole feeling our way along"; "There were times the water was in the cab"
- Miami described in 1926 as "the Magic City because it was growing so fast"; population approximately 75,000; hurricane of September 17 and 18 (1926) caused significant destruction
- Notable Miami landmarks circa 1925–1926: Seminole Indian village on NW 22nd Street; Venetian Pool (originally a coral rock pit, beautified by artist Denman Fink); Roney Plaza hotel (described as "the end of the Beach," torn down approximately five years before 1974); seven big hotels on Miami Beach; one-lane bridge connecting Miami to Miami Beach
- In 1927–1928 tappings, Iron Arrow tapped George LaMere, first student member with full-blooded Indian lineage; member of the Winnebago Tribe; vocalist; Indian name Hotonka meant "big voice" (source: The Miami Hurricane, January 6, 1938, and Spofford Scrapbook, 1927–28, University of Miami Archives)
- First Iron Arrow social gathering held January 30, 1928 — the 90th anniversary of the death of Osceola — at the Casa Alegre
- Source quote on the event: "That exclusive organization, the Iron Arrows, threw their first party at the Casa Alegre today. It is rumored that ladies were present..." (Ibis, 1928; The University News, February 2, 1928)
- Music provided by Dale Clark, Clara Nelle DuPuis, and Katie Bostwick; fortunes told by Louise MacCallman
- Attendees (women): Katie Bostwick, Dorothy Bostwick, Clara Nelle DuPuis, Francis "Peewee" Bolton, Louise MacCallman, Marjorie Welch
- Iron Arrow members present: Harry Gray, Leonard Tuttle, Dale Clark, Ted Kennedy, Bob Fink, Gavin Millar, Francis Houghtaling, Clarke Wilson
- Origin of the University of Miami "Hurricanes" team name: Larry Catha account — "Cub" Buck was the first coach; team went undefeated first year; name proposed by Porter Norris on a bus after a boy on a motorcycle warned players of an incoming hurricane: "let us be the Hurricanes" (source: Catha letter to Rhea Warren, July 11, 1975)
- Key founding dates per Francis Houghtaling (letter to Rhea Warren, July 11, 1975):
  - November 11, 1926 (Thursday): Houghtaling met Dr. B. F. Ashe in the physics laboratory of Dr. O. P. Hart — within one month of the University opening (Friday, October 15)
  - November 15, 1926 (Monday): Houghtaling and Howard Southgate met for the first time
  - November 19, 1926: "The founding nine met in Howard Southgate's office in the NE corner of the auditorium" — first meeting in Iron Arrow history
